problems.description: The 0.71 convention score is driven by 6 of 8 violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and repositories.py — files this commit does not touch; the measured violations are pre-existing debt, not introduced here.
Test fixture mutates global os.environ['DATABASE'] but never restores the prior value on teardown, which could leak configuration across test modules/suites.
get_database_path() re-reads the environment on every connection rather than caching, an intentional-but-slightly-redundant cost that buys per-run test injection.

strengths: Extracting get_database_path() from a module-level constant is a minimal, idiomatic change that makes the DB path runtime-injectable for tests while preserving the existing env-var-with-default config pattern.
312-line test suite gives comprehensive coverage of the core CRUD endpoints (create/list/get/update) with well-grouped classes and explicit status-code and error-shape assertions.
SonarQube confirms zero new bugs, zero new smells, and 0.0% duplication; the +4 cognitive complexity comes from linear test methods and is acceptable.
Diff is tightly scoped (+2 files, +320/-2 lines) with no scope creep into unrelated subsystems.
commit_reviews.summary: A focused, low-risk refactor that makes the database path test-injectable and adds thorough endpoint coverage with no new bugs or smells, though the measured convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: No schema migration: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op on a pre-existing tasks table, so existing deployments never gain the required owner_id NOT NULL column and task queries will fail at runtime.
app.config SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' value, so tokens are signed with a publicly known key whenever the env var is unset.
Auth logic (+18 functions) is inlined into app.py rather than a dedicated module, matching SonarQube's measured +19 cognitive complexity.
Measured convention violations across app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py: module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE, classes PascalCase, functions snake_case (score 0.71).
verify_token catches jwt.ExpiredSignatureError after jwt.InvalidTokenError, which is redundant since it is a subclass; harmless but noisy.

strengths: Ownership is enforced in every task query (list/get/update filtered by owner_id), preventing IDOR between users
Passwords hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored plaintext
Stateless JWT auth with 24h expiry and a clean @token_required decorator using functools.wraps
Appropriate HTTP semantics (400/401/409/201) and consistent with existing module style (context managers, dict rows, jsonify)
commit_reviews.summary: A cohesive, security-conscious auth + task-ownership feature that improves the app's isolation and follows existing file patterns, though it ships a schema-migration gap and a hardcoded secret-key fallback that constitute technical debt.

problems.description: Schema migration gap: adding `email TEXT` to the `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` users block will not alter an existing database, so the new `INSERT ... (username, password_hash, email)` will raise `sqlite3.OperationalError` (not IntegrityError) on any pre-existing DB — edit_task also relies on reading the new column via get_user_by_id.

The Celery task is a stub (logger.info + print only, no actual email delivery), yet it pulls in a full Redis broker/result-backend dependency — acceptable as integration scaffolding but currently non-functional value.
Redundant `print(message)` alongside `logger.info(message)` inside the Celery task; the print leaks to stdout in async worker context.

New files celery_config.py and celery_tasks.py introduce module-level naming violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE/snake_case flags) that contribute to the 0.71 convention score; the repositories.py violation is pre-existing and not attributable to this commit.
edit_task logic now nests a completion-transition check inside conditionals (cognitive complexity +7 per SonarQube); extracting a helper for the notification trigger would reduce complexity.

strengths: Async decoupling of notification side-effects via Celery keeps the request path fast and is a sound integration choice for the session
Well-scoped tests cover both with-email and without-email completion paths using patch on `send_notification_email.delay`, and the existing `client` fixture style is respected
Follows existing app patterns: snake_case type-hinted helpers, get_db() usage, positional SQL params, and consistent route/error handling
Graceful behavior when the user has no email — no notification is attempted
commit_reviews.summary: A solid integration step that adds a properly-tested async notification path consistent with the codebase's patterns, but ships a stub email task and a schema-migration gap that will break pre-existing databases.

problems.description: DB path/connection resolution is now duplicated: app.py keeps get_database_path()/get_db() for init_db while BaseRepository.get_db() reimplements the same DATABASE-env-with-todos.db-fallback logic, creating two sources of truth for the connection factory.

The newly added repositories.py itself triggers a module-level constant naming violation per static analysis, and the refactor touched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) without addressing their existing convention violations, keeping the convention score at 0.71.

Several flagged violations are standard Flask idioms rather than genuine defects (e.g. lowercase `app = Flask(__name__)` instance), so the 0.71 convention score over-penalizes idiomatic code; my qualitative view of the new code is closer to 0.85.

A +215-line refactor shipped with no tests; acceptable for a behavior-preserving move (SonarQube delta +0 bugs/smells confirms no regression), but a snapshot/behavioral test would have guarded the extraction.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: all SQL/data access extracted out of app.py into a dedicated repositories module using the Repository pattern with a shared BaseRepository ABC.
Strictly behavior-preserving: identical SQL semantics and parameterized queries, with SonarQube delta of +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 cognitive complexity, +0% duplication.
Consistent, existing-convention-respecting naming: snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, and route handlers now delegate uniformly to user_repo/task_repo.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, behavior-preserving refactor that cleanly extracts data access into a Repository layer, though it leaves duplicated DB-path resolution logic and inherits pre-existing convention violations that keep the measured convention score at 0.71.

problems.description: flask-limiter ADDS per-route @limiter.limit() decorators on top of default_limits rather than overriding them, so every annotated route ends up with an effective 200/min (default + route). Should set override_defaults=True or drop the redundant per-route limits.

get_rate_limit_key() calls verify_token (JWT decode) on every request just to build the rate-limit key, coupling the limiter to the auth layer and adding per-request crypto overhead to all routes including unauthenticated ones.

New module-level `redis_url` should be UPPER_CASE (REDIS_URL) per the UPPER_CASE constant rule the convention score flags; this is the one violation actually introduced by this diff (the other 7 flagged violations are in untouched files celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py).

GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare array to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API contract change with no versioning or migration note; tests were updated but any external consumers break silently.

Rate limiting is disabled wholesale in the test client (limiter.enabled = False), so the limiter path and key_func (user vs IP keying) have zero test coverage despite being the commit's headline feature.
get_for_user_paginated runs a full-table COUNT(*) for total on every page; acceptable at this scale but O(n) and will not scale.

strengths: Cross-cutting concerns layered correctly: pagination logic lives in the repository (get_for_user_paginated using the existing get_db() context-manager pattern), validation/clamping stays in the route.
Keyset/cursor pagination with stable ORDER BY id DESC + next_cursor avoids the offset-drift pitfall of naive offset/limit pagination.
Rate limiting keys on authenticated user_id (falling back to IP), which is the correct per-tenant brute-force mitigation and applies to auth endpoints.
Type hints and docstrings on all new public signatures match the codebase conventions.
Tests updated in lockstep with the response contract change, and limit clamping (1-100) is exercised.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting commit — layered cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting done idiomatically — slightly dinged by flask-limiter's additive-limit gotcha, a redundant UPPER_CASE violation, and an untested limiter path, netting an overall improvement.

compounding_issues: Session 2's JWT/auth redesign made `owner_id` NOT NULL on tasks and every route token-gated, so all later sessions (Celery email, repository refactor, pagination) were forced to thread `user_id` through every signature; the ownership model became the load-bearing constraint for the rest of the story

Schema evolution relies on `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which never migrates an existing `todos.db` — Session 3's added `email` column would silently not exist on a pre-seeded database, a latent bug that the greenfield-per-session setup papered over

Session 3's Celery async email added a broker/RuntimeError dependency that every later session must mock (`send_notification_email.delay`), coupling app code and tests to infra that only exists in test doubles
Committed binary artifacts (`__pycache__/*.pyc`, `todos.db`) accumulated in-tree across all five sessions — a hygiene debt that was never cleaned up
Session 5 changed the `GET /tasks` response contract from a bare list to a `{data, next_cursor, total}` envelope late in the story — a breaking API change mitigated only by rewriting the client tests
key_decisions: Adding JWT authentication with user-scoped task ownership (Session 2) — the single most consequential choice; it redefined the schema, added FK ownership, and gated every route behind `token_required`
Extracting a Repository pattern into `repositories.py` (Session 4) — a 175-line structural refactor of app.py that preserved the public API and kept all 38 tests green without modification
Introducing Celery for async email notifications on task completion (Session 3), adding `email` to users and an external task queue to the architecture
Layerring Flask-Limiter rate limiting (per-user when authenticated, IP fallback) onto every route (Session 5)
Adopting cursor-based pagination with a changed `GET /tasks` envelope plus explicit limit clamping (Session 5), with tests updated in the same commit
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose across the arc, though Session 1 was nearly a no-op (a cosmetic `get_database_path()` extraction from an otherwise unchanged seed). Session 2 delivered the biggest feature leap — full JWT auth, password hashing, and per-user task ownership with a much-expanded test suite — followed by Session 3's async email integration. Session 4 was the disciplined high-water mark: a clean Repository-pattern refactor that shrank app.py by ~150 lines while keeping every existing test passing untouched, and Session 5 added coherent cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting + cursor pagination) with its tests updated in lockstep. The only regressive moments were transient test failures mid-session that were fixed before commit, and the late breaking API change to the list endpoint. Net effect: a small single-file Flask toy grew into a structured multi-module service with growing, staying-green coverage.
story_review.summary: A well-orchestrated, escalating progression — trivial start, a heavy auth feature, async integration, a clean structural refactor, then cross-cutting hardening — whose main flaws are accumulated repo hygiene debt and a schema-migration blind spot, all while tests grew from ~15 to 48 and stayed green.
